nameStory: Purple false foxglove gets its name from its tubular purple flowers that resemble those of true foxglove, but it's not actually related to that European garden plant. The 'false' part is key - while it looks similar, this native wildflower belongs to an entirely different plant family and won't give you the heart medication that true foxglove is famous for.
description: Purple false foxglove is a slender annual wildflower that grows 1-4 feet tall with delicate, bright purple trumpet-shaped flowers. The plant has a graceful, open branching pattern with narrow leaves and produces its showy blooms in late summer and early fall. It's a native wildflower that adds vibrant color to meadows and open areas when many other flowers are fading for the season.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright purple trumpet-shaped flowers about 1 inch long with 5 rounded lobes that flare open at the mouth, blooming from late summer into fall

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, linear leaves that feel smooth and are arranged oppositely on the stem, giving the plant a delicate, airy appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, branching annual that grows 1-4 feet tall with an open, graceful form that sways gently in the breeze

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small round capsules that split open to release tiny seeds, often persisting into winter as brown, papery remnants

habitat: Look for purple false foxglove in open meadows, prairies, old fields, and along roadsides throughout New England. It prefers sandy or well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade, often growing alongside goldenrod, asters, and other late-season wildflowers.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in spring, but young plants are small and inconspicuous with just narrow leaves visible.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow taller and more branched through summer, with flower buds forming in late summer.
seasonality.fall: The spectacular purple blooms appear from late August through October, making this the prime identification season.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems with small brown seed capsules may persist, but the annual plants have died back completely.

funFact: Purple false foxglove is actually a sneaky plant thief - it's partially parasitic and taps into the roots of grasses and other plants nearby to steal water and nutrients, which helps explain why it can thrive in poor soils where other flowers struggle.
confusionNotes: The tubular purple flowers might be confused with wild bergamot or other purple wildflowers, but purple false foxglove's trumpet shape with 5 rounded lobes and narrow opposite leaves make it distinctive. Remember: if it looks like a mini purple trumpet in late summer, it's likely your false foxglove.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name, this plant is completely unrelated to true foxglove (Digitalis) and doesn't contain the same heart-affecting compounds. It was moved from the snapdragon family to the broomrape family relatively recently as botanists better understood its parasitic nature.
compareHints: Purple false foxglove is the most common and robust of the false foxgloves in New England, with larger flowers and broader leaves than slender false foxglove. Saltmarsh false foxglove grows only in coastal salt marshes, while the other relatives are much rarer and found in specialized habitats. If you see a false foxglove inland with substantial purple flowers, it's most likely this species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's false foxgloves, slender false foxglove has the thinnest, most thread-like leaves - much narrower than purple false foxglove's broader lance-shaped leaves.
Saltmarsh false foxglove is the only member of its genus that requires salty conditions - this habitat preference makes it the easiest false foxglove to identify.

Tenlobe false foxglove is distinguished from other New England false foxgloves primarily by its flower structure - it has ten corolla lobes versus five in most relatives, and tends to have more deeply divided, thread-like leaves than purple false foxglove.
Compared to its false foxglove relatives, Nova Scotia false foxglove is distinguished mainly by its coastal habitat requirement and very limited range.
Beach false foxglove differs from its relatives like purple false foxglove and slender false foxglove primarily by its coastal habitat and extremely narrow, thread-like leaves.
